API 653 tank inspection: what Atlantis performs and what your inspector decides

For an API 653 tank inspection, Atlantis performs the NDE: shell UT, floor MFL scanning with UT prove-up, corrosion mapping, weld VT, MT and PT, and settlement survey support. ASNT-certified technicians do the work under ASNT Level III oversight. Your API 653 Authorized Inspector plans the inspection, evaluates the data, decides repairs and intervals, and signs the report. Atlantis is not the Authorized Inspector. We send a quote within 24 hours of receiving your tank data.

The NDE scope, component by component

API 653 sets what a tank inspection has to establish. This section covers the practical side: which examinations produce that evidence, and what to write into the purchase order so the data supports your inspector's decisions.

Tank areaNDE we performWhat your inspector gets
Shell coursesUT thickness at the shell CMLs on each course, in service or out of serviceReadings by course and CML, comparable with earlier surveys
Lower course, door sheet and nozzle areasCorrosion mapping with automated UT or PAUT where spot readings scatterThickness grids showing the extent and depth of local loss
Floor platesMFL scanning to the agreed threshold, with UT prove-up of every flagged areaPlate map with indications and confirmed remaining thickness
Annular ring and critical zoneUT, PAUT or corrosion mapping where MFL scanners cannot reachThickness data for the zone next to the shell
Shell-to-bottom weld, nozzle welds and repairsVT, MT and PT; RT through licensed radiography crews where volumetric examination is specifiedWeld results with location, method and acceptance standard
Roof, pontoons and appurtenancesVT, with UT where plate loss is suspectedFindings with photos and thickness where measured
Foundation and settlementSettlement survey support at the points your inspector specifiesElevation data tied to the plate map, ready for the Annex B evaluation

Shell UT

Shell thickness surveys run on fixed CMLs so each survey can be compared with the last. External UT can be taken while the tank is in service, from ground level or from access the owner provides. If the CML register is missing or inconsistent, we propose a layout for your inspector to approve before the first reading. We do not invent one in the field.

Floor MFL with UT prove-up

MFL finds metal loss quickly over large plate areas. UT then measures what MFL flagged. Two numbers belong in the contract: the MFL threshold your inspector has chosen, and the prove-up rule, meaning which indications get UT and how many points per indication. Scanners cannot cover every square inch. The strip next to the shell, lap welds, sumps, column bases and patch plates need UT or other methods. The coverage map in our report shows exactly what was scanned and what was not. Our MFL operators and procedures come with the qualification records your inspector will want to see under API 653 Annex G.

Corrosion mapping

Where single readings scatter, a grid tells the truth. We use automated UT or PAUT C-scans on the lower shell course, around nozzles and reinforcing plates, and on annular plates where local loss is suspected. The output is a thickness grid with its location on the tank, not a single minimum value. See corrosion mapping for the method.

Weld examination

VT covers the shell-to-bottom weld, nozzle welds and visible repairs. MT or PT is applied where your inspector or repair procedure calls for surface examination, for example on cracking suspects or completed repair welds. Every result records the weld or area ID, method, procedure and acceptance standard.

Settlement survey support

Settlement is measured with the tank empty, so it should be planned into the out-of-service window. We support the survey by laying out and recording the points your inspector specifies, or by working alongside your surveyor. The data is tied to the same plate map as the floor results. The Annex B evaluation of the readings stays with your inspector or engineer.

If your inspector wants an independent check of the NDE before signing, our Level III can review the data. The decisions stay with the inspector.

How an engagement runs, step by step

  1. You send the tank list. Data sheets, the last inspection report, product service and your inspector's scope, if it exists.
  2. We scope and quote. Methods, coverage, crew, equipment and days per tank. You get the quote within 24 hours.
  3. Pre-job agreement. Your inspector confirms the CML and plate numbering, the MFL threshold, prove-up rules and any corrosion-mapping areas. We submit procedures, technician certifications and calibration records for acceptance.
  4. Owner preparation. Cleaning, degassing, ventilation, lighting and entry permits are in place. MFL scanning needs a floor clean enough for the scanner to run.
  5. Fieldwork in sequence. Visual survey, then floor MFL, prove-up, annular and shell UT, corrosion mapping, weld examinations and settlement support. Significant findings go to your inspector the same day.
  6. Reports. Method reports reviewed under Level III oversight, with plate maps, reading tables and coverage maps.
  7. Repairs. Once your inspector decides the repairs, we examine them as specified.
  8. Close-out. The data is handed over in your format. It can also be placed on a 3D model of the tank through Digital Twin reporting.

Ready to scope a tank or a tank farm? Request an inspection quote and attach the last report.

NDE deliverables your inspector receives

API 653 lists what the inspection report must contain. The NDE package is what that report is built from. Ours includes:

  • Method reports for each examination, signed by the examiner and reviewed under Level III oversight.
  • A floor plate map with every MFL indication, its prove-up thickness and its position on the plate.
  • A coverage map showing scanned areas, unscanned areas and the reason for each gap.
  • Shell reading tables by course and CML, in the same numbering as your earlier surveys.
  • Corrosion-mapping grids with their location on the tank.
  • Weld examination results with weld IDs, methods, procedures and acceptance standards.
  • Settlement data tied to the agreed points and datum.
  • Supporting records: procedures, technician certifications, Annex G qualification records for the MFL work, and instrument calibration certificates.

Your inspector uses this package to calculate corrosion rates and minimum thickness, decide repairs and set the next interval. Data comes back in your format, so it drops into your existing inspection files without re-keying.

US regulatory overlay: SPCC, STI SP001, PHMSA and California

API 653 is an industry standard. In the US, regulations decide when you must follow it, or something equivalent.

EPA SPCC rule (40 CFR 112)

The SPCC rule generally applies to non-transportation facilities with more than 1,320 US gallons of aggregate aboveground oil storage capacity, counting only containers of 55 gallons or more, where a discharge could reach navigable waters or adjoining shorelines. The facility's SPCC Plan has to name the industry standard used for integrity testing of each container and the qualifications of the people doing it. A licensed Professional Engineer certifies the Plan, unless the facility qualifies to self-certify. Tier I and Tier II qualified facilities hold 10,000 gallons or less in aggregate and meet the rule's discharge-history criteria. The Plan must be reviewed at least once every five years. EPA's guidance says inspection and test records must be kept for three years, and recommends keeping formal inspection records for the life of the container. Where a facility departs from the industry standard with a site-specific program, a PE generally has to certify that it is environmentally equivalent. Tier I qualified facilities cannot deviate.

STI SP001 for shop-built tanks

API 653 is written for field-erected welded steel tanks. Shop-built tanks, such as horizontal fuel tanks, double-wall tanks and small vertical tanks, are commonly inspected to the Steel Tank Institute's SP001 standard instead. SP001 covers welded metal shop-fabricated tanks, small field-erected tanks and portable containers such as drums and totes. It sets the type and frequency of inspection by tank size and configuration, for example whether the tank has secondary containment and a means of release detection. Some configurations need only the owner's periodic visual inspections. Others need formal external and internal inspections by a certified inspector as SP001 defines. Atlantis performs the UT thickness readings and other NDE the SP001 inspector calls for. The formal inspection itself stays with the certified inspector.

PHMSA breakout tanks (49 CFR 195.432)

Hazardous liquid pipeline operators must inspect the physical integrity of in-service atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks according to API Std 653, as incorporated by reference. One exception matters for planning. The risk-based alternative internal inspection interval in API 653 section 6.4.3 cannot be used for these tanks. Intervals come from section 6.4.2.

California APSA

California's Aboveground Petroleum Storage Act applies to tank facilities with 1,320 gallons or more of petroleum and requires an SPCC Plan. Local Certified Unified Program Agencies (CUPAs) administer it, with oversight from the Office of the State Fire Marshal. Expect your CUPA inspector to ask for the integrity testing records your Plan promises.

Edition note: API 653's current edition carries Addendum 4, published July 2025. Confirm which edition and addenda your owner's procedures and your regulator reference before the job starts.

How to choose an API 653 tank inspection company

Many companies say "API 653 tank inspection". Few separate the NDE from the inspector's role clearly. Ask these questions before you award the work:

  • Who signs what? The NDE contractor signs method reports. The Authorized Inspector signs the inspection report. If a bid blurs the two, ask which person holds the API 653 certification and who employs them.
  • What is the MFL threshold, and who set it? It should come from your inspector, not from the scanner's default setting.
  • What is the prove-up rule? Every flagged area, or a sample? How many UT points per indication?
  • Will you get a coverage map? Unscanned areas must be visible, not implied.
  • Are MFL operators and procedures qualified per Annex G? Ask to see the records before mobilization.
  • How are the critical zone and annular ring covered? This is where scanners stop and failures start.
  • Will the data come back against your CML and plate numbers? If not, the next survey cannot be compared with this one.

Common mistakes when buying tank NDE

  • Booking the MFL crew before cleaning is finished. Scale and sludge stop the scanner and waste crew days.
  • Forgetting the settlement survey. It needs the tank empty, so it belongs in the out-of-service window.
  • Accepting a floor report with no prove-up depths. An MFL indication without a UT value cannot support a remaining-thickness calculation.
  • Letting each contractor renumber CMLs and plates. The next survey then cannot be compared with this one.
  • Buying on price per tank alone. Coverage, threshold and prove-up rules decide what the price actually buys.

For the full code background, read the API 653 tank inspection guide.

Frequently asked questions

Who performs an API 653 tank inspection: Atlantis or our inspector?

Both, in different roles. Your API 653 Authorized Inspector conducts or supervises the inspection, evaluates the data and signs the report. Atlantis performs the NDE that produces the data. Atlantis is not the Authorized Inspector.

What NDE does an API 653 internal inspection usually need?

Typically floor MFL scanning with UT prove-up, UT of the annular ring and critical zone, shell UT by course, corrosion mapping where loss is local, visual examination of welds and appurtenances, surface examination where specified, and a settlement survey. Your inspector sets the final scope.

How do we choose an API 653 tank inspection company?

Check that the bid separates NDE from the inspector's role, names the MFL threshold and prove-up rule, provides a coverage map and reports against your CML and plate numbers. Ask for Annex G qualification records for the MFL crew.

Does API 653 apply to shop-built tanks?

API 653 is written for field-erected welded steel tanks. Shop-built tanks are usually inspected to STI SP001, as named in the facility's SPCC Plan. We perform the NDE either standard calls for.

What does an MFL tank floor inspection not cover?

MFL scanners cannot reach the strip next to the shell, lap welds, sumps, column bases or patch plates, and MFL alone does not size remaining thickness. Those areas need UT or corrosion mapping, and every MFL indication needs UT prove-up. A coverage map shows what was and was not scanned.

Do you repair tanks?

No. Repairs are done by a repair contractor under a plan your inspector approves. We perform the NDE of the repairs your inspector specifies.

Do you offer API 653 inspector training?

No. Atlantis training is ASNT SNT-TC-1A only, for Level I, II and III NDT technicians, delivered live online or onsite at the employer.

How quickly can we get a quote?

Within 24 hours of receiving the tank list, data sheets and last report. Request an inspection quote to start.

Can the results go into a digital model of the tank?

Yes. Floor, shell, annular and settlement data can be placed on a 3D model of the tank, campaign by campaign. Request an inspection quote and ask for the 3D handover.
